Hook: In 1992 Stan Shih, the founder of Acer, the Taiwanese computer maker, sat down to work out where the money in his industry was made. He went link by link: the operating system, the processor, the memory and the drives at one end; putting the computer together in the middle; the brand, the selling and the service at the other. 'As I drew the curve of the value added that I analyzed,' he said, 'it turned out to result in a smile-shaped curve.' High at both ends. And in the middle, the lowest point: 'The curve showed manufacturing is the lowest in terms of value.' He drew it to persuade his own staff that moving assembly out of Taiwan would cost them nothing that mattered.

Thirty-four years later the curve can be read straight from two sets of accounts. Hon Hai of Taiwan, better known as Foxconn, makes phones, servers and computers for other companies' brands. In 2025 its revenue was NT$8.1 trillion, about $260 billion. It kept 2.3 cents of every dollar as profit. Apple, which designs devices and has them made by partners like Hon Hai, had $479 billion of revenue in its latest year, and kept 28 cents of every dollar. The company that builds the device takes in a fortune and keeps almost none of it.
Industry, Built. Part sixteen: electronics. Why does the company that builds the device keep the least of it?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: the order that needs a plant.

You run an assembler, a company that builds devices for other people's brands. A brand offers you an order: 20 million devices a year for 3 years, at $30 a device for assembling and testing them. The catch: it wants a new plant, ready in a year. The plant costs $800 million. Each device costs you about $12 in labour, power and logistics, and the plant costs $60 million a year to keep open. After three years the brand will either renew for three more, or move the work to someone else. It will not tell you which.

Here is the plant's cash, year by year. Year zero: you spend $800 million building it. Year one, the line is still learning, and runs at half speed: about $120 million. Years two and three, at full speed: about $300 million each. Add it up in today's money and the order alone leaves you about $194 million short. Only if the brand renews do the later years arrive, and then the plant is worth about $420 million. Thirty dollars a device sounds like plenty; on a plant that may stand idle in three years, it is not.

So the decision is a bet on the brand. Across: the chance it renews. Up: what the plant is worth today. Declining is worth nothing either way. Building is worth it only if you put the chance of renewal above about 32 per cent. And a plant in a new country, with cheaper labour but a slower start, pays only if renewal is likelier still. That is the assembler's life: the brand holds the customer and the design, and can take the work elsewhere; the assembler holds the plant. Whoever can walk away keeps the margin.

There is a way out, and it shows who holds the power. If you pay for the plant and the brand walks away after three years, you are about $194 million down. If the brand pays for half of it, the tools and the special equipment, the same three years leave you about $206 million up. A brand that wants a plant built quickly can pay for the tooling, and then the assembler no longer needs to trust it. Whoever pays for the machines carries the risk that the work moves away.
Making: Chapter two. From design to box.

A device starts as a design, but it is built in a few hours on a line like this. A bare circuit board enters. A printer lays solder paste through a stencil onto its pads. A pick-and-place machine sets the chips and the tiny resistors and capacitors onto the paste, many thousands an hour. An oven melts the solder, and cameras check every joint. Then final assembly: the board goes into the case with the screen, the battery and the cameras, mostly by hand. Every device is tested, boxed and shipped. Almost every part on that board was made by someone else; the line's own contribution is the putting together.

How many come off lines like that? Take one country's purchases. In 2025 the United States imported about 141 million smartphones, declared at the border at about $372 each on average. And about 100 million laptops, at about $492. That is the value declared at customs, as the devices arrive; the price in the shop is higher.

Who does that work? Very often not the company whose name is on the box. Apple's annual report says that substantially all of its hardware is made by outsourcing partners, primarily in China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. The partners are companies most people have never heard of. Flex, one of the big contract manufacturers, employed about 149,686 people in more than a hundred facilities across some thirty countries, building for other companies' brands.
Dollar: Chapter three. Where the device's dollar goes.

Follow the money from a $900 device, built by the Works in round numbers. About $450 buys the parts: the chips, the screen, the battery, the cameras, the case. Their makers keep perhaps a quarter of that, $112. The assembler is paid $30 for putting it together and testing it. The brand spends about $160 a device on design, software, marketing and selling, and keeps the rest, $260. Now plot what each link keeps. The parts makers, about $112; the assembler, after paying for its people and its plant, about $15; the brand, $260. Shih's smile, from the arithmetic.

Not every brand sits on that right end. Take a cheaper phone from the Works: $300, with $210 of parts, a $12 assembly fee and $60 of the brand's own costs. The parts are most of the price, and the brand keeps $18, 6 per cent, against 29 per cent on the dearer device. A brand that cannot charge much more than its parts cost sits nearly as low as its assembler.

And in real accounts? Three makers of components: Amphenol, which makes connectors, kept about 18 cents of every dollar in 2025; TE Connectivity about 11; Corning, the glass maker, about 10. Three assemblers: Hon Hai, Jabil and Flex, two to three cents each. And the brands: Apple, 28 cents. But not every brand sits on the high end. HP and Dell, whose personal computers are built from the same standard parts as everyone else's, keep only a few cents. The right end of the smile is for brands that own something others cannot copy.
Contract: These are the contract manufacturers that file accounts in America: Jabil, Flex, Sanmina, Plexus, Benchmark and Celestica. Here is the profit each kept from a dollar of revenue, year by year since 2010. Fifteen years, booms and busts, and they have stayed almost entirely between zero and five cents. Hon Hai, the biggest of them all, kept about two cents. How does a business live on so little?

Part of the answer is in the bookkeeping. Most assemblers buy the parts themselves and sell the finished device to the brand. Their revenue includes every chip and screen, so the Works' assembler books about $9.6 billion of revenue for 20 million devices, and its profit of $300 million is a margin of about 3 per cent. If the brand supplied the parts instead and paid only for the work, the same profit would be 50 per cent of a much smaller revenue. Nothing about the business changed, only what counts as revenue. The thin margin is partly an illusion of passing other people's parts through the books.

The other part is speed. Hon Hai kept about 2.3 cents of each dollar of sales in 2025. But each dollar of its assets turned over about 1.6 times a year in sales. And it finances its assets partly with what it owes suppliers and lenders. Multiply them and its owners earned about 10 per cent on their equity. Its inventory was about 53 days of costs, and it spent 1.5 per cent of revenue on research. An assembler is a machine for turning capital over fast, not for keeping much of each turn.

And it is a business of people as well as plants. Flex counted about 61,841 people in the Americas, 60,870 in Asia, and 26,975 in Europe. Only 16 per cent of its sales were made in China. Flex builds for many industries, not just phones, and spreads its plants across about thirty countries, close to the customers it builds for.
HonHai: Chapter five. Hon Hai in its own numbers.

Hon Hai's own accounts say what it makes. In 2024 its biggest line was smart consumer electronics, phones, televisions and game consoles: about NT$3.2 trillion. Servers and networking brought in NT$2.0 trillion. In 2025 servers and networking jumped 63 per cent, to NT$3.26 trillion, and overtook the phones, which slipped. The company best known for assembling phones now takes in more from building the machines that fill data centres.

And for whom. In 2024 a single customer, which the accounts call only 'Client E', brought in 54 per cent of Hon Hai's revenue. In 2025, with the servers growing, that customer's share fell to 44 per cent. Still nearly half of the biggest assembler's business, from one brand. That is the other side of the thin margin: whoever brings that much work can set the price of it.

Where are those customers? The accounts sort revenue by where each customer is registered. 45 per cent came from customers registered in the United States, 22 per cent from Singapore and 11 per cent from Ireland: not where the factories are, but where those customers' companies are registered. China, where so many of the plants are, accounted for 5 per cent. The factory is in Asia; the customer is a brand registered somewhere else.

Even inside Hon Hai the smile shows. Its server and networking arm, Foxconn Industrial Internet, a separately listed company in Shanghai, made about 4.7 cents of operating income on each dollar in 2025. The rest of the group, where the phones and computers are, made about 1.4. In 2025, building servers paid more than three times as well, per dollar of sales, as building phones and computers.
Brand: What does the brand own? First, the design and the name. In its fiscal 2026 Apple sold about $356 billion of devices, and kept 39.3 per cent of that as gross margin after paying for the parts and the assembly. Second, the devices already in people's pockets. Selling services to their owners brought in $123 billion, at a gross margin of 76.2 per cent. The phone is sold once; the services are sold every month to everyone who bought one.

And the second business keeps growing in weight. Apple's products earned a gross margin of 37.2 per cent in fiscal 2024 and 39.3 in 2026; its services, 73.9, then 76.2. Services were 26 per cent of its sales in fiscal 2026, but 40 per cent of its gross margin. The device opens the account; the account keeps paying.

Put the two side by side. Apple's profit in its latest year: about $132 billion. Hon Hai's, the largest of its assemblers: about $6 billion, on about half Apple's sales. And the dependence runs one way. Hon Hai's largest customer brought it 44 per cent of its revenue; Jabil's, 20 per cent. A brand can split its orders between assemblers; an assembler cannot easily replace a customer that size. That is what Shih's smile measures: not who works hardest, but who can be replaced.
Components: The left end of the smile is crowded too, and not every part pays. Amphenol and TE Connectivity make connectors and sensors: thousands of small, specified parts that a design engineer picks once and rarely changes. In most years they have kept ten to twenty cents in the dollar. Corning, the glass maker, and ASE, which packages and tests chips, a little less. Then displays. LG Display makes panels for televisions, laptops and phones, in factories that cost billions. It lost money in 6 of the 10 years shown, and in every year from 2022 to 2024. A screen is a commodity bought by the square metre, made in plants that keep running when prices fall: the memory cycle, again.

What makes a part pay is whether it can be replaced. A phone holds a processor, memory, a screen, cameras, a battery, a modem, glass and connectors. Apple's annual report says most of its components are available from more than one source, but that certain ones come from a single source or a few. And in 2026 it reported supply constraints and rising costs for advanced chips, memory and storage: the part makers' turn to set the price. The left end of the smile belongs to whoever makes a part nobody else can.

In 2026 the part that set the price was memory, the boom of the semiconductors film. TrendForce, a market tracker, estimated that memory was about a tenth of the parts' cost of a top iPhone in 2025. For the 2026 model it put the share at about a third, 34 per cent, and the parts' cost about 38 per cent higher. These are a tracker's estimates, not Apple's figures; Apple's own report says only that memory costs rose. When a component is scarce, its maker can raise its price, even to the most powerful buyer.
Intermission: An intermission, and one line from America's consumer price index. Prices in general have risen about 12 times since 1951. The government's price index for televisions, which allows for the better sets each year buys, has fallen 99.4 per cent. After inflation, 99.95 per cent. The television went from a luxury to something almost every household could afford. A set built from standard parts, which many factories can make, gets cheaper year after year.

The same index tells the story of the other boxes. Computers: down 96 per cent since 1998. Smartphones, which the index has tracked on their own only since 2021: down 48 per cent already. These are quality-adjusted: a faster computer at the same price counts as a cheaper one. Year after year, better factories and better parts have reached the buyer as lower prices.

One more line: what America's own computer factories produce, measured, like the prices, with allowance for quality. The Federal Reserve's index is about 7,543 times its 1972 level. In the same years the jobs making computers and electronics roughly halved. Better machines and better chips multiply what each factory turns out, with fewer people.
PC: Chapter eight. The PC, the earlier case.

Shih drew his curve about the personal computer, and the computer still fits it. A PC is assembled from standard parts: anyone can buy the same processor, memory and operating system. The maker of the processor, Intel's PC chip business, kept 29 cents of operating income on each dollar of sales in 2025, and more the year before. HP, one of the largest makers of the computers themselves, kept about 5 cents. Dell, about 6. The parts that cannot be swapped earn the money; the box that anyone can put together does not.

And the market itself barely grows. America imports about a hundred million laptops a year: 108 million in 2015, 138 million in the pandemic year of 2021, 100 million in 2025, at an average declared value of about $492. A market that does not grow, built from parts anyone can buy, leaves the box makers with thin margins, as HP's and Dell's show.

HP shows the same curve inside one company. Its computers brought in $39 billion in fiscal 2025 and earned 5.3 cents on the dollar. Its printing business brought in less than half that, $17 billion, but earned more in total: $3.1 billion, 19 cents on the dollar. $11 billion of that revenue was ink and toner: the part bought again and again, for a machine only one company's cartridges fit.
Servers: Chapter nine. The new box: servers.

Now the box that changed the business. Here is what America imported of computer processing units, the customs category that holds servers, each year since 2015. For years it ran at twenty to forty billion dollars, mostly from Mexico. Then the data-centre boom: $62 billion in 2024 and $165 billion in 2025. From Mexico, $81 billion; from Taiwan, $70 billion, up from $8 billion two years before. And from China, which supplied $5.6 billion in 2018: $0.4 billion. The servers are built close to the buyer, or where the chips are made.

The companies that build them grew with them. Supermicro, an American server maker, sold about $3.5 billion in its fiscal 2019 and $39 billion in the year to June 2026. Celestica, a Canadian contract manufacturer, grew from $7.2 billion to $12.4 billion in three years. And Hon Hai's cloud and networking line rose by 63 per cent in a single year. And, as Hon Hai's own segments showed, building servers pays better, for now, than building phones.

Did the boom fatten the builders' margins? A little. Celestica kept 2.5 cents in the dollar in 2022 and 6.7 in 2025. Supermicro has swung between about two and nine cents. And Hon Hai's server arm earned 4.7 cents of operating income. Better than building phones, but still the bottom of the smile. The money in a server goes to the chips inside it: Nvidia, as the last film showed, kept 71 cents of gross margin on each dollar it sold.

The same shift shows inside one brand. Dell began reporting the servers it builds for artificial intelligence separately. They brought in about $1.9 billion in its fiscal 2024, $9.3 billion the next year and $24.7 billion in the year to January 2026. Its server, networking and storage group earned 11.7 cents of operating income per dollar; its personal computers, 5.6. For now, the new box pays for the brand as well as for the builder.
Cluster: Chapter ten. The cluster, and the move.

Where are the assembly plants? Hon Hai's accounts list its plants, equipment and other long-lived assets by country. At the end of 2024, by far the most were in China: about NT$295 billion. A year later China's had shrunk a little, while Vietnam's rose by half, America's by 39 per cent, Mexico's by 33, and India's by 18. Even so, China still held more than Vietnam, America and India put together. Assembly does move, but one plant and one product at a time.

One country stands out for the American market: Mexico, across a land border. America's imports of servers and processing units from Mexico went from $17 billion in 2017 to $81 billion in 2025. Its televisions held at about $9 billion, most of America's. Its laptops, from almost nothing to $3.3 billion. And Hon Hai's own assets in Mexico grew by a third in a single year.

And America's own electronics factories? In 1990 about 1.9 million Americans worked making computers and electronic products. In 2025, about 1.0 million: roughly half, while the country bought more electronics than ever. The assembly happens elsewhere, as the trade figures in the next chapter show.
Tariffs: Chapter eleven. Tariffs and the reshuffling of the chain.

Since 2018 America has tried to move this chain with tariffs. In June 2018 it put a 25 per cent duty on a first list of Chinese goods. In August 2019 it announced duties on most of the rest, but delayed those on goods where China supplied three-quarters or more of America's imports. Phones and laptops were such goods: China supplied 82 and 94 per cent of them in 2018. That December the delayed duty was suspended before it began. In the spring of 2025 came new tariffs on imports from almost everywhere, China, India and Vietnam included, as Apple's annual report records. In January 2026 an investigation into chips imposed nothing new on Apple's products, and on 20 February the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs imposed under emergency powers; Apple applied for refunds.

Here are America's imports of mobile phones. From 2015 to 2024, China supplied about three-quarters or more of them, tariffs or no tariffs. Then in 2025, the year of the new tariffs, China's phones fell to $24 billion, from $42 billion, and India's rose to $22 billion. India's share went from almost nothing in 2018 to 42 per cent in seven years, most of it in the last two.

Count the phones rather than the dollars. In 2024 about 118 million smartphones came to America from China; in 2025, about 61 million. From India, 15 million, then 51 million. From Vietnam, 7 million, then 25 million. Tens of millions of phones a year changed country of assembly in twelve months.

And laptops. China supplied more than nine in every ten until 2022. Then they moved, fast: by 2025 China's share was 18 per cent, and Vietnam's $30 billion was the largest. The tariffs of 2018 hardly moved the laptop; the years since 2023 did.

In units the laptop's move is starker still. From China, about 74 million laptops in 2024 and 23 million in 2025. From Vietnam, 22 million, then 56 million. Thailand and Mexico, from almost none to 10 and 5 million. America bought about as many laptops as ever; they simply came from somewhere else.

Televisions show where a big, cheap, bulky box ends up. In 2017 America imported about $13 billion of them, $8.4 billion from Mexico and $4.1 billion from China. In 2025, $9.0 billion of $11 came from Mexico, and almost none from China. Most of America's televisions now cross a land border, close to the people who buy them.
Landscape: First, scale. Hon Hai took in about $260 billion in 2025. The six contract manufacturers that file accounts in America took in about $98 billion between them in their latest years. Hon Hai alone is more than two and a half times their size.

The landscape, as of November 2026. Across: revenue in the latest year. Up: profit kept per dollar, averaged over five years. The brands: Apple far above the rest, about 26 cents; Sony, Logitech, HP and Dell much lower. The assemblers, from Hon Hai, the largest by far, to Jabil, Flex, Sanmina, Celestica, Plexus and Benchmark, all in a thin band near the bottom; Supermicro, the server maker, a little higher. And the component makers: Amphenol and TE well up the chart, Corning and ASE between, LG Display below the line. Beyond the chart, with no American filings: Samsung, Xiaomi, Lenovo, Luxshare, BOE, the Taiwanese assemblers Pegatron, Quanta and Wistron, and Japan's Murata and TDK.

What to watch. Where America's phones come from: India's share, which brings us to our call. Servers, and how long the data-centre build-out keeps the assemblers busy. Tariffs: the refunds after the Supreme Court's ruling, and whatever replaces them. Memory, whose soaring price Apple already names as a cost. Hon Hai's biggest customer, and whether its share keeps falling. And the laptop's move out of China, which happened in three years after five of standing still.
Called: Two forecasts. The first was made on television in April 2025, the week of the new tariffs. America's Commerce Secretary said that 'the army of millions and millions of human beings screwing in little screws to make iPhones, that kind of thing is going to come to America', automated. What happened? In 2025 America imported $52 billion of smartphones, about the same as the year before. But from China, $24 billion, down from $42; from India, $22 billion. And American jobs making computers and electronics did not rise. Called it? Not so far. The screws moved, but to India, not to America.

Now our own call, written down so you can check it. Here is India's share of America's smartphone imports, month by month since January 2025. It passed half in the spring of 2025. Then from September to December it fell back, as China supplied the launch months of the new phones. In 2026 India has been above half every month so far: 58 per cent from January to August. If the last four months of 2026 look like the last four of 2025, the year ends at 50.1 per cent: a coin toss around one half. India's shipments this year have run well above last year's, and we think that tips it. We give it 55 per cent, and we will check it against the 2026 trade figures, right or wrong.

Here is the arithmetic behind the call. Across: India's share of America's smartphone imports in the last four months of 2026. Up: its share of the whole year. To end the year above half, India needs about 38 per cent of those last four months. In the same months of 2025 it had 39 per cent. So the call comes down to whether India supplies more of this autumn's new phones than it did last year's.
Outro: Back to the question: why does the company that builds the device keep the least of it? Put the year's accounts in a row, from the makers of the parts to the assemblers to the brands. Shih's smile is still there, thirty-four years on. The assembler keeps little because almost anyone with a plant and a workforce could do its job, because one brand can bring it half its business, and because the plant stays when the order leaves. The ends keep more when they own something that cannot be swapped: a part nobody else makes, or a name and a set of services that customers come back to. Where they do not, as with the PC makers, the brand end sags too.

And the newest box draws the same curve. The maker of its chips, Nvidia, kept 71 cents of gross margin on the dollar. The assembler, Hon Hai's server arm, about 5 cents of operating income. The brand that sells the finished server, Dell's server group, about 12. The measures differ, but the shape does not: deep in the middle, high where something cannot be swapped.

Electronics, in five answers. What is sold is a device built from other companies' parts, under a brand, and then the services sold to everyone who owns one. It is made on lines that place, solder, assemble and test, mostly by contract manufacturers in Asia. The dollar goes to the brand and to the makers of parts nobody else can make, and very little to the assembler. It stays there because the brand holds the customer and can move the work, while the assembler holds the plant. And what moves it are new boxes, like the servers of the data-centre boom, and tariffs, and the slow move of assembly from China to India, Vietnam and Mexico. Next time: cars, and why it is so hard to make money making them.
